entries.concept: Shift-left security and Policy as Code
entries.description: Integrate security at every SDLC phase: Plan (Threat Modeling), Code (SAST), Build (SCA, Trivy), Test (DAST), Release (SBOM, Snyk), Deploy (Config Audit), Monitor (Runtime Alerts). Use Policy as Code with OPA/Conftest to enforce rules declaratively — e.g. deny if Docker image has no USER or no HEALTHCHECK.
decision_rules: Apply security controls at the earliest feasible phase — finding issues in Code is 10x cheaper than in Production
Express security policies as code (OPA Rego, Conftest) so they are versioned, testable, and automated
tradeoffs: Shift-left adds tooling and process overhead in early phases — offset by significantly reducing costly late-stage remediations
anti_patterns: Running security scans only in a pre-production gate — too late in the cycle
Manual security reviews without automated policy enforcement
aws_alignment: Use AWS Config Rules and Security Hub to enforce policies at the infrastructure layer

entries.concept: SAST tools for static code security analysis
entries.description: Recommended SAST tools by language: Semgrep (multi-language, OWASP + custom rules), Bandit (Python, B1xx-B7xx rules: bandit -r ./backend -ll -f json -o bandit-report.json), SpotBugs/FindSec-Bugs (Java), ESLint Security plugin (JS/TS), CodeQL (multi-language, taint tracking). Export results as SARIF for GitHub Security tab integration.
decision_rules: Run Semgrep with p/python and p/owasp-top-ten configs as the baseline for Python projects
Export SARIF format (semgrep --sarif > semgrep.sarif) for GitHub Security tab visibility
Add CodeQL for deeper taint-tracking analysis on critical codebases
tradeoffs: SAST tools generate false positives — tune rules and triage findings before making them pipeline blockers
CodeQL analysis is slower than Semgrep — run on schedule or PR, not every commit
anti_patterns: Running SAST on test code only — scan production application code
Suppressing all SAST findings without documented risk acceptance
aws_alignment: Integrate Semgrep SARIF results with Amazon CodeGuru for unified findings

entries.concept: Secrets management — scan and retrieval best practices
entries.description: Prevent secrets from entering version control using pre-commit hooks with gitleaks (v8.18.0) and trufflehog (v3.63.0). For runtime secret retrieval in Python, use boto3 to call AWS Secrets Manager get_secret_value — never load secrets from environment variables or config files.
decision_rules: Install gitleaks pre-commit hook in every repository to block secret commits before they happen
Use AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault for runtime secret retrieval — never pass secrets as env vars
Add trufflehog --only-verified to catch high-confidence secrets that evade simpler regex scanners
tradeoffs: Pre-commit hooks only protect developers who have installed them — enforce via CI/CD as a backstop
anti_patterns: Storing secrets in .env files committed to git
Passing secrets as command-line arguments (visible in process list and shell history)
Loading secrets from environment variables injected at container startup without a vault
aws_alignment: Use AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation for database credentials
Use Secrets Manager resource policies to restrict secret access to specific IAM roles

entries.description: Generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for every Docker image using Syft (syft myapp:latest -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json). Analyze the SBOM with Grype (grype sbom:./sbom.spdx.json --fail-on high). Alternatively use CycloneDX format (cyclonedx-py environment -o sbom.cyclonedx.json).
decision_rules: Generate SBOM in the build stage and store it as a CI artifact alongside the image
Use grype --fail-on high to block promotion of images with HIGH severity CVEs in dependencies
Prefer SPDX or CycloneDX formats for tooling interoperability
tradeoffs: SBOM generation adds ~30 seconds to the build — acceptable for the supply chain transparency gained
anti_patterns: Deploying images without knowing their dependency inventory
Not re-scanning SBOMs after new CVEs are published — CVEs are discovered continuously
aws_alignment: Store SBOMs in Amazon S3 alongside image tags for traceability
Use Amazon Inspector for continuous CVE scanning of ECR images

entries.concept: Container image signing and verification with Cosign
entries.description: Sign container images with Cosign (Sigstore): cosign generate-key-pair, cosign sign --key cosign.key myregistry.io/myapp:1.0.0. Verify before deployment: cosign verify --key cosign.pub myregistry.io/myapp:1.0.0. Enforce signature verification in Kubernetes with Kyverno ClusterPolicy (verifyImages).
decision_rules: Sign every image pushed to production registry — signing proves the image came from a trusted CI pipeline
Use Kyverno ClusterPolicy with verifyImages to reject unsigned or untrusted images at admission time
tradeoffs: Cosign keyless signing (Fulcio + Rekor) is simpler but requires OIDC identity — good for GitHub Actions
Key-based signing requires secure storage of the private key (use KMS-backed keys)
anti_patterns: Deploying images from public registries without verifying their provenance
Using mutable image tags (latest) in production — makes signature verification unreliable
aws_alignment: Use AWS Signer for ECR image signing as an alternative to Cosign on EKS

entries.description: Use Falco for runtime behavioral detection in containers and Kubernetes. Define custom rules to detect unexpected outbound connections (condition: outbound and not proc.name in allowed_processes). Alerts on anomalies: unexpected shells, file system writes, privilege escalation, data exfiltration patterns.
decision_rules: Deploy Falco as a DaemonSet on every Kubernetes node for runtime visibility
Define an allowlist of expected processes and IPs — alert on any deviation
Route Falco alerts to SIEM (Splunk, Elasticsearch) or AWS Security Hub for centralized analysis
tradeoffs: Falco kernel module/eBPF probe adds small CPU overhead — use eBPF mode for lower overhead
Default Falco rules generate significant alert volume — tune and create suppression rules for known-good behavior
anti_patterns: Relying solely on pre-deployment scans with no runtime security monitoring
Running Falco with default rules only without tuning — alert fatigue reduces effectiveness
aws_alignment: Use Amazon Security Lake and Amazon Detective for incident investigation of Falco alerts
GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring is an AWS-managed alternative to Falco on EKS

entries.concept: Threat modeling with STRIDE for REST APIs
entries.description: Apply STRIDE threat model to REST API design: Spoofing (mitigate: JWT/mTLS auth), Tampering (mitigate: HTTPS + request signing), Repudiation (mitigate: immutable audit logs via CloudTrail), Information Disclosure (mitigate: encryption + log filtering), Denial of Service (mitigate: rate limiting + WAF + circuit breakers), Elevation of Privilege (mitigate: RBAC + permission validation per request).
decision_rules: Run STRIDE analysis for every new API endpoint or significant feature change
Map each threat to a concrete control — do not leave any STRIDE category without a mitigation
tradeoffs: Threat modeling sessions add time to the design phase — run lightweight threat model reviews (1-2 hours) rather than exhaustive sessions
anti_patterns: Skipping threat modeling and relying entirely on reactive vulnerability scanning
Treating threat modeling as a one-time exercise — repeat for significant architectural changes
aws_alignment: Use AWS Threat Composer as a structured threat modeling tool aligned with AWS services

entries.description: Phase CODE: pre-commit hooks (secret scan, linting), threat modeling for new features, dependency pinning with hashes. Phase BUILD: SAST (Semgrep, Bandit, CodeQL), SCA (Safety, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check), Dockerfile lint (Hadolint), Docker image scan (Trivy, Grype), SBOM generation. Phase TEST: DAST (OWASP ZAP, Nuclei), auth/authz tests, input fuzzing. Phase DEPLOY: IaC scan (tfsec, Checkov), secrets via Secrets Manager, signed images (Cosign), policy enforcement (OPA/Kyverno). Phase MONITOR: runtime security (Falco), anomaly alerting (GuardDuty, Security Hub), credential rotation, privileged access audit.
decision_rules: Treat this checklist as a minimum — automate as many items as possible in CI/CD
Track checklist completion per release in a security runbook
tradeoffs: Automating all checklist items requires significant initial tooling investment — prioritize CODE and BUILD phases first
anti_patterns: Running only one security phase (e.g. SAST only) and skipping others
Not reviewing checklist after a security incident — update it with lessons learned
aws_alignment: AWS Security Hub security score tracks many of these controls automatically across AWS services
